full_judgment:
4. It is at this juncture that the Pre-emptee-Petitioner puts this Court on notice of the history of the two rounds of proceedings and cases stemming from Miscellaneous Case No. 45 of 1987 and culminating in the impugned judgment and order dated 31.3.1997 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1994. The matter at issue now, however, according to the Pre-emptee-Petitioner is given that the provisions of Section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') mandates that a pre-emptor must make parties of co-sharer tenants of holdings and tenancies contiguous to the land transferred, the Pre-emptor's case has from the very beginning been marked by a defect of non-joinder or non-addition of such parties, and the lower appellate court having at the very last stage failed to appropriately determine that matter on the basis of facts and evidence before it, the judgment and order in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1994 is now liable to be set aside. 

 6. The Lower Court Records (LCR) have been particularly illuminating in charting the trajectory of the two rounds of proceedings and cases stemming from Miscellaneous Case No. 45 of 1987 with regard to the matter at hand. A perusal of the impugned judgment in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1994 reveals how the issue of the joinder or addition of necessary parties was dealt with both by the trial court and the parties at the initial round. Reading the impugned judgment in conjunction with the relevant documents in the LCR it is evident that on 28.8.1988 interrogatories pertaining to non-joinder of necessary parties were addressed to the Pre-emptee to which a response was made on 17.12.1988. The application pertaining to the reply being allowed on 13.2.1989, the Pre-emptor, acting under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, applied on 7.3.1989 for the addition of parties in keeping with the reply so submitted by the Pre-emptee and this was allowed. This provided the essential basis upon which Miscellaneous Case No. 45 of 1987 was initially disposed of on 26.6.1989 resulting in a dismissal of the pre-emption application with a finding that one Fanaullah, ostensibly a co-sharer by purchase from the Pre-emptor's husband, had not been made a party to the case. The LCR reveals that in so disposing of that case the trial court proceeded upon statements given both by the said Fanaullah as D.W.2 and an ostensible admission to that effect by the Pre-emptor P.W.1. A clear reading of that statement of the Pre-emptor given on cross-examination and with objection shows, however, that it falls short of a categorical endorsement of the claimed status of the said Fanaullah as a co-sharer by purchase. The trial court, nevertheless, considered that statement of the Pre-emptor to be of overriding value. Be that as it may, the said decision of the trial court, thereafter, came to be considered in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 1989 filed by the Pre-emptor. 

 8. A notable feature of these two judgments, the Learned Counsel for the Pre-emptor-Opposite Party No. 1, Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, now submits is that these constitute concurrent findings as to the rights of the Pre-emptor-Opposite Party No. 1 against the Pre-emptee-Petitioner. It is evident that both these concurrent judgments found on a consideration of all facts and evidence that since the Pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the suit land and the Pre-emptee is one by purchase in the same, there was no impediment under Section 96 of the. Act for the Pre-emptor to file the pre-emption case. The outstanding issue that, thereafter, came to be determined by both the courts below was the extent to which, if at all, the Pre-emptor's case suffered from a defect of parties. In that regard as well, both the courts below were in agreement as to the absence of any such defect. In this regard, Mr. Huq has at the outset submitted on the established principle that interference in revisionary jurisdiction with concurrent findings of the lower appellate and trial courts is not admissible when such findings are based on a proper appreciation of evidence as, for example, held by the Appellate Division in Rupe Johan Begum vs. Lutfe Ali Chowdhury reported both in 1 MLR (AD) (1996), 374 and 49 DLR (AD) (1997), 73. Indeed, interference in the case of concurrent findings of fact is permissible in revisionary jurisdiction only exceptionally in circumstances where there has been a misreading or non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case as held in Amanatullah vs. Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan 2 BLC (AD) (1987) and/or where the resultant decision appears in any way perverse being contrary to the evidence on record. Moreover, the contention that concurrent findings of facts are immune from attack in exercise of revisionary jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code, came to be considered by the High Court Division in Abdul Kader Bari vs. Kaiser Ahmed Howlader reported in 4 BLC (1999) HCD, 17 resulting in the following succinct encapsulation of the revisional court's modus operandi in such circumstances at paragraph 29, page 26: 

 It is well recognized that the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below are not liable to be disturbed by this Court in exercise of power under section 115 of the Code. This Court in exercising Revisional Jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code can only interfere if it is shown that the finding is based on gross misreading or non-consideration of material evidence or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is "perverse" being contrary to the evidence on record. 

 10. This Court finds merit in Mr. Huq's submissions that the principle so enunciated circumscribing the authority to so interfere in revision constitutes the essential premise for determination of the matter at hand. The Learned Counsel for the Pre-emptee-Petitioner Md. Mozammel Hossain has stressed upon the mandatory requirement evident in Section 96(2) of the Act, a non-compliance with which must prove to be fatal to the Pre-emptor's application. In this regard, Mr. Mozammel Hossain has in particular relied upon the Appellate Division's judgment in the case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab Ali reported in 33 DLR AD (1981), 113. Mr. Hossain relies on the said judgment as the basis for the assertion that the thrust of Section 96(2) of the Act is that all the co-sharer tenants or all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred are to be necessarily impleaded and therefore be made to be before the court for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. Mr. Huq, for his part, however, refers to yet another aspect of the same case in what, he submits, aptly bears upon the facts and circumstances of the case at hand. Mr. Huq submits that the principle of impleading necessary parties in a pre-emption case is also to be read and deemed to be circumscribed by the Appellate Division's observations in paragraphs 19, 21 & 22 at page 120-122 of Abdus Samad's Case to the effect that a pre-emptor shall be remiss in not impleading co-sharer(s) and not bringing such co-sharers on record ignoring any objection that may have been taken "at the earliest opportunity" by a pre-emptee, that shall prove fatal for the pre-emptor's case which must, therefore, fail for defect of parties. This Court notes that this aspect of the Appellate Division's judgment in the Abdus Samad's Case has subsequently been relied upon in Zainal Abedin vs. Syed Hasmatullah and others, 4 BLD (1984), 272 to the effect that if a party seeking pre-emption fails to implead a party whose existence is disclosed upon a plea of non joinder having been taken, the right of pre-emption will be deemed to be lost. In Zainal Abedin's Case the matter was one of an initial objection as to a defect of parties and a petition filed thereafter specifically giving names and addresses of co-sharer tenants who were necessary parties but even then were not in fact impleaded. As a result, it was held that notwithstanding the submission of names and address of necessary co-sharers long before the hearing of the case, and there being no evidence of any waiver of the objection as to omission of necessary parties, failure to take steps to implead such co-sharers as parties proved fatal to the pre-emption case. 

 11. In light of the judicial precedents and precepts considered above, it has been this Court's effort to ascertain the extent to which a non-consideration of the Pre-emptor's legal responsibility to so implead upon a plea of or objection as to defect of parties being taken by the Pre-emptee as well as a misreading or misconstruction of the Pre-emptor's actions in this regard in the impugned judgment and order in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1994 constitute any error of law resulting in an error in that decision occasioning a failure of justice. In this regard, while the concurrent finding of facts is evident on the face of the impugned judgment, the possibility of a "gross misreading or non-consideration of material evidence or...misconception or mis-application of law or misinterpretation of any material document" as observed in Abdul Kader Bari's Case above, has been a matter of enquiry by this Court. As noted earlier, this Court found the impugned judgment of the Learned Subordinate Judge an accurate guide to the history of the pre-emption case as initiated in 1987 and the relevant documents of the LCR in ascertaining the extent of the effort on the part of both the courts below to determine the extent of the Pre-emptor's compliance with the mandatory requirement of impleading necessary parties in a pre-emption case as this. This Court notes that both the Pre-emptor, on one hand and the two courts below, on the other, have been particularly mindful of the necessity of impleading co-sharer tenants to the extent possible. In this regard, the Pre-emptee Petitioner had a key role to play and conducted himself accordingly at all stages of the pre-emption case. The Pre-emptee's role was importantly duly complemented in compliance at all stages by that of the Pre-emptor, with the courts below for their part never having abdicated their responsibility of oversight of the necessity and process of impleading necessary co-sharer parties. This case clearly distinct, for example, from Zainal Abedin's Case, was one case where the Pre-emptor-Opposite Party No. 1 duly responded to an objection of defect of parties and complied by impleading those as were brought to the attention of the court by the Pre-emptee-Petitioner. It is also noted complementing this exercise were both the courts below that at all stages remained vigilant at detecting any outstanding or residual defect of parties and took necessary action in this regard to secure the presence of necessary co-sharer tenants as parties before the courts. While the trial court came to a finding on the necessity to the Fanaullah as a necessity party, the lower appellate court in its decision dated 28.4.1993 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 35 of 1989 found one Mohfizuddin to be the more appropriate candidate for such selection for addition as a co-sharer tenant by inheritance. In allowing the Pre-emptor's appeal the case was sent on remand for further action and decision in that regard. A perusal of the LCR in general and the two decisions given in the first round by the two courts reveals that both courts proceeded upon due consideration of facts and evidence available before each and proceeded to decide accordingly. The lower appellate court's judgment given in this first round having necessarily come to prevail, Mohfizuddin was accordingly, impleaded as is evident by way of subsequent application made by the prayer Order 1 Rule 10 is on 6.10.1993. From then onwards the case embarked on its second round of determination both by the trial and the lower appellate court resulting in the judgments with which this Court is now concerned. This Court is of the view that in a nutshell, this is a case where the courts and the parties concerned satisfactorily acted concertedly in the discharge of their mutually reinforcing obligations to save the pre-emption case from a defect of parties. The complementarity of these mutually reinforcing roles is well enunciated in Abdus Samad's Case at paragraph 19, pages 120-121 thus: 

 "Order 1, rule 10 provides for addition of party at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party. Where there is non-joinder of a necessary party the Court is empowered to add the necessary party under rule 10 at any stage of the proceeding either upon or without the application of either party. The objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant. Such objection provides an opportunity to the plaintiff to remove the defect by adding parties who were omitted. In taking objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties the defendant is required to furnish the names and particulars of the parties who were omitted from the suit. On the refusal of the plaintiff to implead the parties mentioned in the written statement the question becomes an issue for adjudication by the Court and on adjudication the question becomes decided. In such an event the consequences must follow, that is, the suit becomes liable to be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary party. In the case of a pre-emption proceeding the law regarding procedure can-not be treated as different. If the pre-emptee or for that matter any of the parties disclose existence of a necessary party and furnishes the necessary particulars, but the pre-emptor still insists not to implead him as a party, consequence on adjudication is the same." 

 12. The Appellate Division's enunciation above also exposes the pitfalls of non-performance of all or any of the roles so assigned. It is the view of this Court that in the facts and circumstances of this case due performance by all concerned protected the Pre-emptor's case from any such unwarranted pitfall. This Court finds that this is also the view reflected in the judgment impugned in this Application. 

 13. A perusal of the judgment of the Learned Additional Sub-Judge in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1994 reveals that the issue of non-joinder of the parties was indeed still kept alive even at this stage and come up for the lower appellate court's consideration. In that regard, the lower appellate court took note of the history of this case so far as pertained to the issue of defect of the parties as well as the judgments delivered in Abdus Samad's Case reported in 33 DLR (AD) (1981),113 and Zainal Abedin's Case reported in 4 BLD (1984) 272.
